title: CODO: An Automated Compiler for Comprehensive Dataflow Optimization
evidence_span: The paper presents an automated compiler for FPGA dataflow accelerators. It detects and removes coarse- and fine-grained dataflow violations, optimizes on-chip and off-chip data movement, and automatically schedules designs to balance performance and resource use. The reported results include 1.45x–4.52x latency speedups on computation kernels, 3.7x–33.8x speedups on DNN models, 7.3x average speedup on CNNs, and 2.07x speedup on GPT-2; the artifact is publicly released.
problem: Manual construction of efficient streaming FPGA dataflow accelerators remains difficult even with high-level synthesis because dataflow legality, communication efficiency, and resource/performance tradeoffs interact.
method_or_artifact: CODO compiler built around systematic coarse- and fine-grained dataflow-violation detection and repair, on-chip/off-chip data-movement optimization, automatic scheduling, and a public artifact implementation.
workload_or_benchmark: Typical computation kernels, DNN models, CNN models, and GPT-2 evaluated through synthesis and on-board FPGA experiments.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: FPGA dataflow accelerators and high-level-synthesis tool flows; the public evidence does not establish applicability to ASIC implementation or all FPGA families.
metrics: 7.3x average CNN speedup in on-board evaluation
limits: The evidence is an author arXiv preprint plus public artifact documentation; the repository has not independently reproduced synthesis or board results, extracted every baseline/configuration, or established generalization beyond the reported FPGA flows.

title: Patterns Behind Chaos: Forecasting Data Movement for Efficient Large-Scale MoE LLM Inference
evidence_span: The study profiles data movement across four 200B–1000B MoE models using more than 24,000 requests, analyzes temporal and spatial expert-selection behavior, distills six design insights, and applies them to wafer-scale GPU modifications and a prefill-aware expert-placement algorithm. It reports 6.6x average speedup on wafer-scale GPUs and up to 1.25x speedup on existing GPU MoE computation, with profiling traces released publicly.
problem: Random expert selection in large Mixture-of-Experts inference creates data-movement overhead that can dominate serving systems.
method_or_artifact: Data-movement-centric temporal/spatial profiling, distilled placement insights, lightweight wafer-scale architectural modifications, and a prefill-aware expert-placement algorithm.
workload_or_benchmark: Four 200B–1000B MoE models released in 2025, more than 24,000 requests across diverse workloads, wafer-scale GPU architectures, and existing GPU systems.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Wafer-scale GPU and multi-GPU serving systems; reported architectural gains depend on the evaluated expert-selection traces and target topology.
metrics: up to 1.25x speedup on existing GPU MoE computation
limits: The evidence is an author preprint and released trace dataset; the repository has not independently checked the six insights, reproduced the wafer-scale model, or tested whether the placement conclusions transfer to other MoE routing distributions and interconnects.

title: OASIS: Outlier-Aware LUT-Based GEMM with Dual-Side Quantization for LLM Inference Acceleration
evidence_span: OASIS uses Cartesian-product lookup tables to perform GEMM between non-uniformly quantized weights and activations without dequantization. It reports a 64x LUT-size reduction and 1024x higher parallelism over prior LUT-based GEMM, adds outlier-aware activation quantization with error compensation, and introduces the Orizuru top-k outlier-detection engine. The abstract reports 1.98% average accuracy drop versus FP16, 3.00x speedup, and 1.44x energy-efficiency improvement over FIGLUT.
problem: LLM inference must reduce memory and compute cost, but weight-only quantization adds dequantization overhead and integer weight/activation quantization can degrade model quality; non-uniform quantization is difficult to map to conventional low-precision units.
method_or_artifact: Outlier-aware dual-side non-uniform quantization, Cartesian-product LUT-based GEMM without dequantization, concurrent error compensation, and an Orizuru top-k outlier-detection engine.
workload_or_benchmark: LLM inference with non-uniformly quantized weights and activations; comparisons against FP16 accuracy and the FIGLUT accelerator.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Dedicated low-precision accelerator implementing LUT-based GEMM and real-time outlier detection; area, memory, and technology assumptions require primary-paper table verification.
metrics: 1024x higher computational parallelism than existing LUT-based GEMM
limits: The evidence is an author preprint abstract; model suite, sequence lengths, area/energy accounting, accuracy metric, and hardware implementation details must be extracted from the full paper before generalizing the reported gains.

title: DisDP: Disaggregating Compute, Network, and Storage for Model-Sharded Data-Parallel Training
evidence_span: DisDP identifies serial interference among GEMM, network collectives, and optimizer-state storage in model-sharded data parallelism. It fully disaggregates compute, network, and storage, offloads collectives to SmartNICs and SmartSwitches, and uses a SmartSwitch-enhanced parameter server. The abstract reports 3.98x improvement over state-of-the-art training systems on eight GPUs training a 175B model.
problem: Model-sharded data-parallel training reduces GPU memory requirements but adds AllGather and ReduceScatter overhead and interference among compute, communication, and optimizer-state storage.
method_or_artifact: Fully disaggregated compute/network/storage architecture, SmartNIC and SmartSwitch collective offload, and a SmartSwitch-enhanced parameter server for optimizer-state storage.
workload_or_benchmark: Model-sharded LLM training, including a reported 175B model on eight distributed GPUs; the abstract references Llama and DeepSeek-style pretraining workloads.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Multi-GPU distributed training with programmable SmartNIC/SmartSwitch infrastructure and parameter-server storage; topology and failure assumptions require full-paper verification.
baselines: model-sharded data parallelism with conventional GPU-managed collectives
metrics: 3.98x improvement on eight GPUs for a 175B model
collective execution time increase of 41% under aggregated compute/network/storage interference
fewer than 10% of GPU SMs occupied by collectives in the motivating analysis
limits: The evidence is an author preprint abstract; exact baseline systems, network topology, storage cost, parameter-server scaling, failure behavior, and reproduction beyond eight GPUs remain to be verified.

title: Lit Silicon: A Case Where Thermal Imbalance Couples Concurrent Execution in Multiple GPUs
evidence_span: Lit Silicon identifies thermally induced straggling coupled with concurrent computation and communication as a source of multi-GPU performance variation. The study proposes analytical performance and power models, detection and mitigation techniques, and evaluates three power-management strategies on two AMD Instinct MI300X systems, two workloads, and two LLM-training frameworks. It reports up to 6% performance and 4% power improvements.
problem: Thermal imbalance across GPUs can create hotter, slower stragglers that slow cooler leader GPUs during overlapped computation and communication, reducing node-level efficiency.
method_or_artifact: Lit Silicon performance/power models, detection and mitigation techniques, and evaluation of TDP-constrained power optimization, node-level GPU power capping, and CPU power sloshing.
workload_or_benchmark: Two workloads on two AMD Instinct MI300X GPU systems using two LLM training frameworks.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Single-node multi-GPU LLM training with concurrent computation and communication; evidence is specific to evaluated AMD MI300X systems and management policies.
limits: The evidence is an author preprint abstract; workload details, thermal traces, statistical variance, absolute energy, and the claimed datacenter cost implications require full-paper verification and broader hardware replication.
